description:
Somos BioStellar, un equipo de estudiantes apasionados por la ciencia y la tecnología, unidos por el deseo de aportar soluciones que contribuyan al bienestar humano fuera de la Tierra.
En el marco de este reto, trabajamos en una propuesta enfocada en el monitoreo de signos vitales de los astronautas durante misiones espaciales.
summary:
As BioStellar we creat Astra, an installable web application designed to monitor astronauts' physical and mental health in space. It features two modes: Astronaut View (main interface) and Simulation View (for demonstrating various clinical scenarios). The system begins with a manual mode where the astronaut enters their data to establish a baseline. From the main page, they can navigate through menus for:
•	Check-up and Trends: Step-by-step guidance for taking measurements and inputting data.
•	Radiation Monitoring: Tracking of environmental exposure.
•	Baseline and Emergencies: Parameter updates and critical action protocols. The entire process is guided by Stella, an integrated AI virtual assistant.
The platform empowers astronauts to self-manage their health. It guides them step-by-step through clinical measurements and evaluates data without ionizing radiation, explaining why each tracked parameter matters in microgravity and enabling immediate action against anomalies.
In the harsh space environment, the body experiences accelerated decline, such as bone density loss and oxidative stress. Having a real-time, autonomous, and safe monitoring system is vital to prevent irreversible damage, ensure rapid emergency response, and safeguard crew health during long-duration missions.
details:
ASTRA (Astronaut Self-health Tracking & Risk Assessment) is an installable web application that allows astronauts without medical training to check their own health during a mission. At the beginning, they record their baseline—meaning their normal values before leaving Earth. Every day, they perform a guided eight-step check-up: pulse, blood oxygen, blood pressure, temperature, urine test strip, mental state, exercise, and sleep. Each measurement can be taken using an automatic device or entered manually, and the app compares it against healthy ranges and the user's personal baseline. Results are explained in simple language using color codes, along with recommended next steps. The app also displays trends throughout the mission and tracks radiation (baseline, acute, and cumulative against NASA’s career limit). Upon detecting a critical value, it triggers a step-by-step emergency protocol that can be read aloud. It works offline and is available in both English and Spanish.

Astra enables users to:

  • Detect health changes early without depending on an onboard doctor or immediate communication with Earth.
  • Translate medical numbers into clear instructions: what the value means and what to do.
  • Compare data against each astronaut’s individual baseline, rather than just general ranges.
  • Continue operating during connection drops by saving data directly on the device.
  • Guide the crew through emergencies using short steps and hands-free text-to-speech reading.
  • Bring vital signs, rest, mental state, and radiation exposure together in a single place.

Our impact lies in granting medical autonomy to crews on long-duration missions to the Moon or Mars, where communication with Earth is delayed and help cannot arrive quickly. We aim to enable any crew member to assess their health, recognize a warning sign, and act correctly within the first few minutes. This same approach can be applied on Earth for isolated locations or areas lacking close access to healthcare personnel.

To build this application, we used the following tools:

  • Languages: JavaScript (React with JSX), HTML, and CSS.
  • Frameworks and Libraries: React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and React Router.
  • Web Technologies: Service worker and manifest for offline installation and usage, browser local storage, Web Speech API for text-to-speech reading, and Canvas for device signal processing.
  • Collaboration and Deployment: GitHub, Vercel, and Miro.
  • Artificial Intelligence: Claude (Anthropic) as support for prototyping and code; the concept, medical ranges, and protocols were developed entirely by the team.
  • Hardware: None physical. Measuring devices and simulation-mode astronauts are simulated and clearly marked as such within the app.
  • References: NASA-STD-3001 standard for radiation limits and biomedical team research for ranges and protocols.

Astra is not a dashboard for medical doctors: it is designed for someone without a background in health, so each screen asks a single question and responds with a concrete action. We combine daily check-ups, personal baseline comparison, radiation tracking, and voice-assisted emergency protocols into a single tool. Stella, the app's assistant, accompanies the user throughout the experience.

The factors we considered include:

  • Users may be tired, stressed, or alone.
  • Connections can fail, which is why the app works completely offline.
  • A measuring device may fail to respond, so after 15 seconds it automatically switches to manual data entry.
  • The crew is international, which is why the app is bilingual.
  • The app guides rather than diagnoses: it always refers users back to the flight surgeon or ground medical team.
  • Because the team combines computer science and biomedical engineering, we carefully prioritized medical backing and responsible data usage.

During development, we realized how difficult it is to find real, detailed crew data like the metrics our app requests, as space biomedical information is often heavily fragmented or restricted. Therefore, we designed ASTRA not only as a care tool, but also as a means to easily and structuredly collect data, creating reliable databases for future scientific research. Information is one of the most valuable resources in existence, and building reliable sources from these missions is an opportunity we simply couldn't miss.
